trivia_fact: Ansible uses Jinja2 for templating, the same engine used by Flask and Django. This was chosen because Ansible is written in Python, and Jinja2 was already well-known in the Python community. Variables in double curly braces {{ }} come from Jinja2 syntax.

Ansible's "ad-hoc" command mode (running one-off commands without a playbook) was inspired by the Unix philosophy of doing one thing well. The term "ad hoc" is Latin for "for this purpose" — a quick, purpose-specific command rather than a reusable playbook.

Ansible Vault, introduced in version 1.5, allows encrypting sensitive data within playbooks and variable files using AES-256. The "vault" metaphor — a secure place to store valuables — was chosen over alternatives like "safe" or "keychain."

Ansible's handler/notify pattern was inspired by event-driven programming. Handlers only run when notified by a changed task, preventing unnecessary service restarts. This was a direct response to the inefficiency of unconditionally restarting services after every configuration run.

Ansible Collections (introduced in Ansible 2.9) moved modules and plugins from a monolithic distribution to namespaced packages. This solved the "big ball of mud" problem where the core Ansible package contained 3,000+ modules and grew unsustainably large.
